result.title: Motion in One Dimension: Lecture Notes

elements.text: These notes describe motion along a straight line. We track where an object is, how far it has moved, and how quickly its position changes. Every quantity comes with a unit, and checking units is the fastest way to catch a mistake in a calculation.
Position is measured from a chosen origin. When a cart moves from an initial position ⟦p1-e4⟧ to a final position ⟦p1-e5⟧, its displacement is the change in position:
Displacement has a direction. A cart that ends up behind its starting point has a negative displacement, even though the distance it travelled is positive.
Positions and displacements are measured in metres. A displacement of 3 m to the left is written as ⟦p1-e10⟧ when the positive direction points right.
Average velocity is displacement divided by the time taken. For a trip that lasts ⟦p1-e13⟧, the average velocity is ⟦p1-e14⟧, and its unit is metres per second.

elements.text: Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes. A cart that speeds up from rest to 6 m/s in two seconds has an average acceleration of ⟦p2-e2⟧.
When the acceleration is constant, the velocity grows by the same amount every second and a graph of velocity against time is a straight line.

Near the surface of the Earth, a dropped ball has a nearly constant downward acceleration ⟦p2-e7⟧ as long as air resistance is small. Timing a fall over a known height is a simple way to estimate it in the lab.
